name: Avis venosa
note: A speculative field note written by Claude. The species is invented; the natural history of every part it is made from is real.
mythology: In the first autumn the trees let go of all their leaves at once, and nothing came to eat them. They lay on the forest floor so long that they rotted down to their veins, and only then were they light enough for the wind. The wind practised with them for a whole winter. In spring a dragonfly lent its wings for bones, a slime mould gave its pink beads for a skull, and a beaded lizard from a dry valley gave its legs, because it had more patience than speed. The laced bird is what the wind made out of everything the forest had finished with, which is why it is only ever seen in autumn, flying low over the leaves it came from.
lineage: Its wings and tail are skeleton leaves, the vein-lace of flowering plants, a lineage about 130 million years old. Its wing bones are older: dragonfly wings, whose ancestors flew Carboniferous swamps some 300 million years ago. So the laced bird's bones are more than twice as old as its feathers. Its legs come from one of the rarest lizards on earth, the Guatemalan beaded lizard, which lives wild in a single dry valley.
habitat: Deciduous woodland in autumn, at the height of the canopy and again at the level of the leaf litter. Its skull is wolf's milk, a slime mould that fruits on rotting logs, so it never strays far from fallen wood.
behaviour: It flies only when the leaves fall, and folds its leaf-wings flat to rest among them, where it is almost impossible to see. Its spine is made of Venus flytraps, so it startles only when touched twice. In winter it goes still, like the water bears that make its eyes, and waits.
